---
title: "Reference"
subtitle: "Everything the tabset plugin does."
description: "The complete tabset behaviour: the step order, the attributes and classes, accessibility, how a tabset is exported to PDF, and the relation to Quarto's tabset-fragments option."
---

## Enabling the plugin

```yaml
format:
  revealjs: default
revealjs-plugins:
  - tabset
```

Tabsets are written exactly as they are anywhere in Quarto.

## Attributes and classes

| Attribute | Written on | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `tab-active` | A tabset marked `.no-tabset-fragments` | Which tab is open when the slide arrives, counting from zero, so `1` is the second tab. Emitted as `data-tab-active`. |
| `tabset-skip-pdf-clone` | A slide | Keep this slide's tabset on one PDF page rather than one page per tab. |
| `.no-tabset-fragments` | A tabset | Leave this tabset out of the stepping. |

: The attributes and the class. {.striped .hover tbl-colwidths="[24,22,54]"}

A `tab-active` that is not a whole number, or that names a tab the tabset does not have, falls back to the first tab.
`tab-active` and the `.active` class on a tab heading are ignored on a tabset that steps, because the first step always shows the first tab.
A tabset with one tab is left alone.

## Step order

The arrow keys and the space bar step through the tabs and the fragments of a slide in document order, forwards and backwards.
A tab arrives on one step, and the fragments written inside it arrive on the steps after it.
A fragment in a later tab is therefore shown after its own tab, never before.

Fragment indices that you write with `data-fragment-index` keep Reveal.js's rule: indexed fragments come first, in ascending order, and the others follow in document order.

The state of the tabset follows the step, for every slide with a stepped tabset and not only the current one.
Going back, opening a link to a fragment, or clicking another tab and then pressing the arrow key all show the tab that belongs to the current step.
When the step switches the tab, the keyboard focus stays where it was, unless it was on a tab of that tabset.
In the scroll view every tabset shows its last tab, because all the steps are shown.

Several tabsets on one slide are navigated one after another.
A tabset with `.no-tabset-fragments`, and a deck with `fragments: false`, are not stepped.

## Accessibility

The plugin does not write roles, `aria-selected` or `tabindex` values.
Quarto's tabs set them, and the plugin only clicks the tab that belongs to the step.
The Tab order and the Home and End keys on a focused tab work as they do on any Quarto tabset.

The invisible element that carries a tab's step is hidden from assistive technology.

## PDF export

Under Quarto's default, `pdf-separate-fragments: true`, a stepped tabset has one page per step.
Each page shows the tab of its step, and the page numbers are those of Reveal.js.

With `pdf-separate-fragments: false`, the slide is copied once per tab state, following the same steps as the browser.
Nested tabsets and several tabsets on one slide get one page for each tab state they can show, not one page for each tab of the largest tabset.
The copies are numbered `N.1`, `N.2` and so on.
Their `id` values get the suffix `-print-k`, and the links, `aria-controls`, `aria-labelledby` and `for` values that point to them follow, so the document has no duplicate `id`.
Scroll positions inside the slide are copied to each page.
Every tab is kept, whatever `pdf-max-pages-per-slide` says.

Opt a slide out with `tabset-skip-pdf-clone`, which keeps its tabset on a single page showing the first tab.
It does nothing when `pdf-separate-fragments` is `true`.
A tabset marked `.no-tabset-fragments` also prints on one page showing the first tab.

## Quarto's tabset-fragments option

Quarto has a `tabset-fragments` option that does the same work.
When it is on, the extension logs one line to the browser console and does nothing, so the two never step the same tabset twice.
Remove the extension, or turn the option off, to choose one of them.

## Limitations

- RevealJS only.
- The stepping needs JavaScript; without it, Quarto's own tabset behaviour remains.
